question: A 35-year-old man from Chennai develops dengue haemorrhagic fever during a second dengue infection confirmed to be a different serotype from his first infection 2 years ago. Which immunological mechanism best explains the increased severity of this second infection?

answers.text: Antibody-dependent enhancement: non-neutralising IgG from the first infection facilitates viral uptake by macrophages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In ADE, IgG antibodies raised against the first dengue serotype cross-react with but fail to neutralise the second serotype. These sub-neutralising antibodies bind the virus and then engage Fc receptors on monocytes/macrophages, enhancing viral entry and replication. The resulting higher viral load drives greater cytokine release and the vascular leak that characterises dengue haemorrhagic fever.

answers.text: Cross-reactive Th1 cells cause autoimmune destruction of vascular endothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While cross-reactive T cells may contribute to cytokine storms in secondary dengue, the primary mechanism driving increased viral replication and disease severity is ADE — sub-neutralising IgG from the first infection enhances viral uptake into macrophages via Fc receptors, amplifying viral load.

answers.text: Complete absence of immunological memory from the first infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Immunological memory is very much present — that is precisely the problem. Memory B cells produce cross-reactive IgG antibodies that recognise but cannot neutralise the new serotype. These sub-neutralising antibodies mediate antibody-dependent enhancement, paradoxically increasing macrophage infection and viral load.

answers.text: The second serotype produces a more virulent NS1 protein that directly destroys platelets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While NS1 protein does contribute to dengue pathology, the key mechanism in severe secondary dengue is antibody-dependent enhancement. Sub-neutralising cross-reactive IgG from the first infection facilitates viral entry into macrophages via Fc receptors, amplifying viral replication and cytokine-mediated vascular leak.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review ADE: sub-neutralising cross-reactive IgG from a prior infection enhances viral uptake into macrophages via Fc receptors, increasing viral load and disease severity in secondary dengue.
Excellent! ADE is a critical concept — the immune system's memory paradoxically worsens the disease, which is why dengue vaccine design must ideally cover all four serotypes simultaneously.
